title: Constructor Overloading
summary: Provide multiple constructors with different parameter signatures so callers can create objects flexibly with varying amounts of data.
learningObjectives: Define what constructor overloading means in Java
Identify how Java distinguishes constructors by their parameter count and types
Provide multiple convenient entry doors to create the same entity
Predict which constructor executes based on argument list
expectedOutcomes: Ability to write 2 or 3 overloaded constructors for a single class
Complete confidence in resolving constructor signatures at compile time

analogy.headline: A hotel offers multiple check-in methods depending on what you have ready
analogy.story:
When checking into a luxury hotel, there are different ways guests arrive:

1. **Express VIP Guest:** You already booked online, so you just show your name.
2. **Standard Guest:** You show your name, passport ID, and room preference.
3. **Walk-in Guest:** You have no reservation, so you take the standard default room.

All three guests end up with a room, but the hotel provided **multiple front doors** to accommodate different amounts of information!

In Java, **Constructor Overloading** is giving your class multiple front doors. A user can create a `Student` with no data, with just a name, or with a name, age, and course.
analogy.keyTakeaway: Constructor overloading allows a class to have multiple constructors with different parameter lists, giving callers flexible ways to instantiate objects.

activities.title: The Rules of Constructor Overloading

keyTakeaways: Overloaded constructors must share the exact same name (the class name)
Each overloaded constructor must have a UNIQUE parameter list (different count, types, or order)
Constructors CANNOT be differentiated by return type (since they have none)
Java resolves the correct constructor at compile time based on the arguments supplied

questions.prompt: What is constructor overloading in Java?
options: Creating a constructor that takes too much memory
Defining multiple constructors in the same class with different parameter lists
Calling a constructor repeatedly inside an infinite loop
Overriding a parent constructor in a subclass
questions.explanation: Constructor overloading means having multiple constructors in the same class with different parameter signatures.

hints.hint: Multiple constructors in one class.

questions.prompt: How does Java distinguish between overloaded constructors?
options: By their return types
By the number, types, and sequence of their parameters
By their variable names (e.g. x vs y)
By the order in which they appear in the file
questions.explanation: Constructors are distinguished purely by parameter count, types, and sequence.

hints.hint: Parameter data types matter, not names.

questions.prompt: Can two constructors in the same class have the signature: 'Student(String a)' and 'Student(String b)'?
options: Yes, because 'a' and 'b' are different parameter names
No, because both constructors accept the exact same parameter type (String)
Yes, but only if one is public and the other is private
Yes, if they assign to different fields
questions.explanation: Java ignores parameter names when matching signatures. Both are 'Student(String)', creating a duplicate constructor error.

hints.hint: Types are identical: both accept one String.

options: Compile error
questions.explanation: The literal 5 is an integer, so Java matches the exact int parameter constructor, printing '1'.

hints.hint: 5 is an int literal.

questions.prompt: What happens if you call: 'new Sample(5.0)' with the class from the previous question?
options: It prints '1'
It prints '2'
It crashes at runtime
It prints '5.0'
questions.explanation: 5.0 is a double literal, which matches 'Sample(double a)', printing '2'.

hints.hint: 5.0 is of type double.

questions.prompt: Can two constructors differ only by their parameter order, e.g. (int, String) vs (String, int)?
options: Yes, Java treats (int, String) and (String, int) as completely different signatures
No, order of types does not matter
Only in Java 17 and newer
No, this causes ambiguity in all cases
questions.explanation: Parameter sequence is part of the method/constructor signature. (int, String) differs from (String, int).

hints.hint: Type order is strictly checked by the compiler.

questions.prompt: When is constructor overloading resolved by the Java runtime environment?
options: It is NOT resolved at runtime; it is resolved at compile time by javac
When the garbage collector sweeps memory
When the user interacts with the app
During JVM shutdown
questions.explanation: Overloading is a form of compile-time (static) polymorphism. javac binds the exact constructor during compilation.

hints.hint: Overloading is resolved at compile time.

questions.prompt: Why is constructor overloading useful in application design?
options: It gives callers flexibility to create objects whether they have all, some, or none of the data ready
It prevents other developers from modifying classes
It makes the application run twice as fast
It replaces the need for methods
questions.explanation: Overloading accommodates different user flows (e.g. creating an account with email-only vs full profile data).

hints.hint: Think of the hotel check-in analogy.

questions.prompt: If a class has constructors: `Car()` and `Car(String model)`, what happens if you call `new Car("Sedan", 4)`?
options: Java calls Car(String model) and ignores the 4
Compilation error: no constructor matches (String, int)
Java creates a third constructor automatically
It crashes at runtime
questions.explanation: No constructor matching the signature (String, int) exists, so the compiler rejects the call.

hints.hint: Is there a constructor that takes two arguments?

questions.prompt: True or False: There is no strict limit to how many overloaded constructors a class can have.
options: True, as long as each has a unique parameter signature
False, maximum 3 constructors per class
False, maximum 5 constructors per class
True, but only if they all share the same body
questions.explanation: You can define as many overloaded constructors as your design demands, provided their signatures are distinct.

hints.hint: Unique signatures are the only requirement.

interviewQA.question: What is constructor overloading in Java, and why do we use it?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Constructor overloading is the practice of having more than one constructor in the same class, with each constructor having a unique parameter list (differing by count, type, or order of parameters). It provides flexibility for callers to instantiate objects in different starting configurations.
keyPoints: Same name (class name) with different parameter lists
Enables flexible object construction
Resolved at compile time
commonMistakes: Confusing constructor overloading (same class, different params) with overriding (subclass replacing parent method).

interviewQA.question: Can constructors be overloaded based on return type?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: No! Constructors in Java do not have a return type at all. Therefore, constructor overloading can ONLY be achieved by altering the parameter list (count, types, or order).
keyPoints: Constructors have no return type
Only the parameter list can differentiate them
commonMistakes: Thinking you can differentiate constructors with void vs int.

interviewQA.question: Can two overloaded constructors have the same parameter types in different orders, like (int, String) and (String, int)?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Yes. Java considers the sequence of data types in the parameter list as part of the method/constructor signature. Therefore, (int, String) and (String, int) are treated as distinct signatures.
keyPoints: Parameter type sequence is part of signature
Allowed, but should be used sparingly to avoid confusing callers
commonMistakes: Assuming order does not matter in Java method signatures.

interviewQA.question: Is constructor overloading resolved at compile time or runtime?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: It is strictly resolved at compile time. The Java compiler inspects the arguments provided to the 'new' keyword and determines the exact constructor signature to invoke. This is an example of compile-time (static) polymorphism.
keyPoints: Compile-time (static) binding
Javac matches arguments to parameter types
commonMistakes: Saying dynamic or runtime binding. Overriding is runtime; overloading is compile time.

interviewQA.question: What is the common problem with writing multiple overloaded constructors, and how is it solved?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: The primary issue is code duplication: multiple constructors often repeat the same assignment or validation logic. In Java, this is solved cleanly through constructor chaining using 'this()', where smaller constructors delegate to a central master constructor.
keyPoints: Risk of code duplication across constructors
Solved cleanly using constructor chaining: this(...)
commonMistakes: Copy-pasting identical field assignments into 4 different constructors.

interviewQA.question: What happens if an overloaded call matches multiple constructors due to type promotion (e.g. passing an int when (long) and (double) constructors exist)?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Java looks for the most specific matching type. If an exact match does not exist, Java applies primitive widening (int -> long -> float -> double). If two promotions are equally specific or ambiguous, the compiler emits an 'ambiguous method call' error.
keyPoints: Exact match is prioritized
Primitive widening is applied in closest hierarchy order
Ambiguity causes compile-time error
commonMistakes: Assuming Java randomly picks one of the matching constructors.

activities.title: Lesson 4 Checkpoint
checklist: I understand that constructor overloading means multiple constructors in the same class with different parameters.
I know that Java differentiates constructors by parameter count, types, and order, not variable names.
I can predict which constructor runs based on arguments passed to 'new'.
I know that overloading is resolved at compile time.

practiceProblems.title: Overload an Employee Profile
practiceProblems.description:
Create an `Employee` class with fields `String name` and `int id`.

• Overload 1: `Employee()` sets `name = "Guest"`, `id = 0`.
• Overload 2: `Employee(String n, int i)` sets fields to provided arguments.
• In `Main`, create `e1 = new Employee()` and `e2 = new Employee("Aditi", 101)`.
• Print both employees: `E1: Guest (ID: 0) | E2: Aditi (ID: 101)`.
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Create an `Employee` class with fields `String name` and `int id`.

• Overload 1: `Employee()` sets `name = "Guest"`, `id = 0`.
• Overload 2: `Employee(String n, int i)` sets fields to provided arguments.
• In `Main`, create `e1 = new Employee()` and `e2 = new Employee("Aditi", 101)`.
• Print both employees: `E1: Guest (ID: 0) | E2: Aditi (ID: 101)`.
hints: Employee(String n, int i) assigns name = n and id = i.

practiceProblems.title: Three Overloads for a Product Item
practiceProblems.description:
Provide 3 constructors for a `Product` class (`name`, `price`):

1. `Product()`: sets `name = "Generic"`, `price = 0.0`.
2. `Product(String n)`: sets `name = n`, `price = 9.99` (standard flat price).
3. `Product(String n, double p)`: sets both fields.

In `Main`, create one object with each constructor and print their names and prices.
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Provide 3 constructors for a `Product` class (`name`, `price`):

1. `Product()`: sets `name = "Generic"`, `price = 0.0`.
2. `Product(String n)`: sets `name = n`, `price = 9.99` (standard flat price).
3. `Product(String n, double p)`: sets both fields.

In `Main`, create one object with each constructor and print their names and prices.
practiceProblems.hint: Write three distinct constructors with 0, 1, and 2 parameters.
hints: Check that each constructor sets name and price.

practiceProblems.title: Overload by Parameter Data Types
practiceProblems.description:
Constructors can have the same number of parameters if their data types differ:

• Create `Identifier` class with `String code`.
• Overload 1: `Identifier(int num)` -> sets `code = "NUM-" + num`.
• Overload 2: `Identifier(String str)` -> sets `code = "STR-" + str`.
• In `Main`, test with `new Identifier(404)` and `new Identifier("ABC")`.
• Print: `ID1: NUM-404 | ID2: STR-ABC`.
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Constructors can have the same number of parameters if their data types differ:

• Create `Identifier` class with `String code`.
• Overload 1: `Identifier(int num)` -> sets `code = "NUM-" + num`.
• Overload 2: `Identifier(String str)` -> sets `code = "STR-" + str`.
• In `Main`, test with `new Identifier(404)` and `new Identifier("ABC")`.
• Print: `ID1: NUM-404 | ID2: STR-ABC`.
practiceProblems.hint: One constructor takes 'int num', the other takes 'String str'.
hints: Java matches by data type at compile time.

practiceProblems.title: Model a Circle with Overloaded Radius
practiceProblems.description:
Model a `Circle` class with `double radius`:

• Overload 1: `Circle()` sets `radius = 1.0` (Unit Circle).
• Overload 2: `Circle(double r)` sets `radius = r`.
• Method `double getCircumference()` returns `2 * 3.14 * radius`.
• In `Main`, create `c1 = new Circle()` and `c2 = new Circle(5.0)`.
• Print: `C1: 6.28 | C2: 31.40` (or formatted to 2 decimals).

• Print: `C1: 6.28 | C2: 31.40` (or formatted to 2 decimals).
practiceProblems.hint: Set radius = 1.0 in Circle() and radius = r in Circle(double r).
hints: Main uses printf to format output to 2 decimal places.
